title: Can pollution change a trout’s choice?
hook: Can drug pollution change a trout's choice?
paper_title: Methamphetamine pollution elicits addiction in wild fish
citation: Horký et al. (2021), Journal of Experimental Biology
summary: After eight weeks of methamphetamine exposure, hatchery-reared brown trout showed greater preference for a drug-containing current than control fish in laboratory choice tests, particularly during early withdrawal.
evidence_note: One holding tank per treatment confounds treatment with tank. This laboratory study does not demonstrate wild fish seeking polluted wastewater. The preference measure is not a percentage of individual fish choosing a drug.

scenes.headline: DRUGS IN RIVER WATER?
scenes.speech: Could a drug in river water change a fish's choice?

scenes.headline: INVISIBLE POLLUTION
scenes.speech: Some human medicines and drugs reach streams through treated wastewater.

scenes.headline: 8 WEEKS OF EXPOSURE
scenes.speech: Scientists exposed brown trout to one microgram of methamphetamine per litre for eight weeks.

scenes.headline: THEN, A CHOICE TEST
scenes.speech: Later, they tested whether fish preferred clean or methamphetamine containing water.

scenes.headline: A DIFFERENT PREFERENCE
scenes.speech: Previously exposed fish showed a greater preference for the drug containing current than controls during early withdrawal.

scenes.headline: LAB RESULTS, NOT WILD PROOF
scenes.speech: This was a laboratory study with only one exposure tank per treatment. It does not prove drug seeking in wild rivers.

scenes.headline: THE SCIENCE IS LINKED
scenes.speech: Find the original paper in our research library, and follow Toxic Tales for more.

slides.headline: CAN POLLUTION CHANGE A FISH’S CHOICE?
slides.body: Behind the study: a laboratory experiment with brown trout and methamphetamine. Swipe for the result and its limits.

slides.headline: WHAT THE RESEARCHERS DID
slides.body: Hatchery-reared brown trout received either clean water or a nominal methamphetamine concentration of 1 microgram per litre for eight weeks.

slides.headline: A TWO-CURRENT CHOICE TEST
slides.body: After exposure, fish were held in clean water. Researchers then tested their preference between a clean current and a drug-containing current.

slides.headline: WHAT CHANGED?
slides.body: Previously exposed fish showed greater preference for the drug-containing current than controls during early withdrawal. This is a relative treatment difference, not proof that every exposed fish preferred the drug.

slides.headline: THE LIMITATION MATTERS
slides.body: Only one holding tank was used per treatment. Tank effects and drug effects cannot be fully separated. The study also did not track wild fish seeking wastewater.

slides.headline: READ THE ORIGINAL RESEARCH
slides.body: Horký and colleagues, 2021. Journal of Experimental Biology. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.242145. Find this paper in the Toxic Tales source library. Follow @toxic_tales_eco.
